facts.title: One Of Civilization's First Metals
facts.text: Copper was among the very first metals humans worked, with copper artifacts from around 9000 BCE found in the Middle East. Because nuggets of native copper occur naturally in metallic form, early people could hammer it cold into beads and tools long before they learned to smelt ores. Its use was so transformative that it gave its name to the Copper Age (Chalcolithic), the bridge between the Stone Age and the Bronze Age.

facts.title: Named After An Island
facts.text: The symbol Cu comes from the Latin word cuprum, which itself derives from 'aes cyprium' meaning 'metal of Cyprus.' The Mediterranean island of Cyprus was the Roman Empire's main source of copper, so the metal was literally named after the place it was mined. The English word 'copper' evolved from the same Latin root through Old English 'coper.'

facts.title: Bronze And Brass Builders
facts.text: Copper rarely works alone in history: alloyed with tin it makes bronze, and with zinc it makes brass. The invention of bronze around 3300 BCE was so important it defined an entire era, the Bronze Age, because bronze tools and weapons were far harder than pure copper. These two alloys remain workhorses today in everything from musical instruments to ship propellers and plumbing fittings.

facts.title: Second-Best Conductor Of Electricity
facts.text: Copper conducts electricity better than every metal except silver, which is why roughly two-thirds of all copper produced goes into electrical wiring. Silver is only marginally better but far too expensive for mass use, so copper became the practical champion of the electrical age. This single property is why power grids, motors, and the device you are reading this on all depend on copper.

facts.title: It Turns Green On Purpose
facts.text: Copper does not rust like iron; instead it slowly forms a green coating called a patina, made of copper carbonate and sulfate compounds. This patina actually protects the metal underneath from further corrosion, which is why copper roofs and statues can last for centuries. The Statue of Liberty, sheathed in about 80 tonnes of copper, owes its famous green color to this very process over more than a century.

facts.title: Essential Inside Your Body
facts.text: Copper is a trace nutrient your body genuinely needs, with adults containing only about 50 to 120 milligrams of it total. It is a key part of enzymes that help form red blood cells, build connective tissue, and run your nervous system. Too little causes anemia and bone problems, which is why foods like shellfish, nuts, seeds, and dark chocolate are valued copper sources.

facts.title: Blue Blood Of The Sea
facts.text: While humans use iron-based hemoglobin to carry oxygen, animals like octopuses, squid, lobsters, and many snails use a copper-based protein called hemocyanin instead. Because copper turns blue when it binds oxygen, the blood of these creatures is literally blue rather than red. This adaptation works especially well in the cold, low-oxygen waters of the deep ocean.

facts.title: A Natural Germ Killer
facts.text: Copper surfaces are antimicrobial, killing bacteria, viruses, and fungi that land on them through a process scientists call the oligodynamic effect. The metal releases ions that puncture microbial cell membranes and disrupt their DNA, often clearing germs within hours. For this reason hospitals increasingly use copper-alloy doorknobs, bed rails, and handles to help reduce the spread of infections.

facts.title: Forged In Dying Stars
facts.text: Copper is not made in ordinary stellar burning but is forged in the violent deaths of massive stars, particularly during supernova explosions. Processes that rapidly add neutrons to lighter nuclei build up elements like copper, which are then scattered across space to seed new worlds. Every copper atom in a wire or coin was created in such a cosmic cataclysm billions of years ago.

facts.title: Endlessly Recyclable Money Metal
facts.text: Copper can be recycled over and over without any loss of quality, and a large share of the copper ever mined is still in use today. It has also long been a coinage metal: many 'silver' coins and most modern small change are actually copper or copper alloys, and the US penny is copper-plated zinc. With Chile alone producing roughly a quarter of the world's supply, copper remains one of the most economically vital metals on Earth.
